nodes.content: Design online shard migration for a replicated key-value store with linearizable operations and crash-safe ownership transfer.
requirements: Preserve linearizability and acknowledged writes across retries, network partitions, and one replica crash.
Without failures, sustain ≥80% of migration-free throughput while migrating a shard under continuous writes.

nodes.content: Rate-limit snapshot and committed-log streaming to destination quorum; cut over with consensus epochs after catch-up, fencing source and deduplicating retries.
How does consensus-epoch cutover prevent a partitioned source leader from acknowledging writes after destination promotion?
Fencing an old-config majority before promotion prevents any stale leader from quorum-acknowledging writes afterward, even across partitions.
Durably fence the old quorum, reconcile committed writes, replay them to the destination quorum, and model-check partitioned-leader acknowledgments.
Model-check CutoverFence in TLC with 3+3 replicas, one crash, partitions, and invariants for stale acknowledgments and committed-write survival.
CutoverFence.tla and TLC configuration encode six replicas, crash and partition transitions, and stale-acknowledgment and write-survival invariants.
Run TLC on CutoverFence.tla under single-crash and asymmetric-partition schedules, checking post-promotion stale acknowledgments and committed-write survival.
TLC explored 1.8M states: zero post-promotion old-epoch quorum acknowledgments or lost committed writes under partitions and one crash.
Require durable old-quorum fencing and committed-log reconciliation before promotion; TLC found no safety violations within modeled failures.
Run 3+3-replica partition/crash fault injection across fencing, reconciliation, and promotion; check stale acknowledgments and committed-write survival.
In 1/10,000 injected schedules, delayed pre-fence replication replies let the old leader acknowledge after promotion; destination missed the write.
Replaying all writes found in the fenced old quorum’s logs before promotion preserves delayed pre-fence acknowledgments, even if initially unacknowledged.
How can cutover preserve writes acknowledged through delayed pre-fence replication replies after the source quorum is fenced?
Transfer ownership through joint consensus with quorum-intersecting log barriers; rate-limit snapshot streaming and persist request-ID deduplication.
Implement joint-consensus log barriers and durable deduplication; fault-inject partitions/crashes and benchmark throttled streaming against 80% migration-free throughput.
Extend CutoverFence.tla with joint-consensus barriers, delayed replies, and retry deduplication; model-check both cutovers under partitions and one crash.
Extended TLC explored 2.4M states: joint consensus preserved linearizability and acknowledged writes; old-quorum fencing lost one delayed-acknowledged write.
Can joint-consensus migration sustain ≥80% of migration-free throughput under continuous writes while streaming the snapshot and log?
Capping snapshot and log transfer at 20% of replica egress maintains ≥80% baseline throughput during continuous writes.
Benchmark joint-consensus throughput under continuous writes at 20% egress cap; fault-inject delayed acknowledgments to test fenced-quorum replay for acknowledged-write survival.
At 20% egress, migration sustained 84% baseline throughput; 10,000 delayed-ack trials with full fenced-log replay lost zero acknowledged writes.
Sweep 10%, 20%, and 30% egress caps during 60-minute WriteHot-1 runs; measure sustained throughput ratio and log-catch-up time.
The 60-minute WriteHot-1 run sustained 76% baseline throughput at 20% egress, below the 80% target despite the earlier 84% result.
Start at 20% egress (initially 84% throughput); throttle to 10% below 82% throughput, sustaining ≥80% over 60 minutes.
Implement throughput-triggered egress throttling; run 60-minute WriteHot-1 migrations, measuring sustained throughput, catch-up completion, and cutover latency.
Run 60-minute WriteHot-1 migrations comparing fixed 20% egress against adaptive 20%→10% throttling; record throughput and catch-up completion.
With foreground-write priority, fixed 20% egress sustained 81% baseline for 60 minutes, versus adaptive 83%; both completed catch-up.
Run 60-minute bursty WriteHot-1 trials, checking whether the 82% trigger maintains ≥80% throughput and completes catch-up.
Bursty WriteHot-1 fell to 79% baseline at the 82% trigger; switching at 86% sustained 82% and completed catch-up.
Run 60-minute Zipf-0.9 WriteHot-1 migrations at 82% and 86% triggers; measure baseline-relative throughput, catch-up time, and cutover latency.
Zipf-0.9 runs sustained 81% baseline at the 82% trigger and 84% at 86%; both completed catch-up within 48 minutes.
Adopt foreground-write priority and 20%→10% egress at 86% throughput; bursty and Zipf runs exceeded 80% and completed catch-up.
Stage destination replicas as Raft learners using copy-on-write snapshots, then jointly reconfigure after barrier-index catch-up and deduplication-state replication.
How can destination replicas catch up with continuous writes without disrupting source-quorum acknowledgments before cutover?
A copy-on-write snapshot plus throttled Raft learner replay reaches a barrier index while source quorum continues acknowledging writes.
Implement copy-on-write snapshots and 86%-triggered learner throttling; measure barrier catch-up and source write acknowledgments under continuous writes.
Run 60-minute WriteHot-1 with copy-on-write learner snapshots, 86%-triggered throttling, and dedup replay; measure barrier catch-up and acknowledgment continuity.
WriteHot-1 learners reached barrier catch-up in 42 minutes; source quorum continued acknowledging writes at 83% baseline throughput.
Inject one replica crash and asymmetric partitions during snapshot/replay; verify quorum-gated acknowledgments and learner barrier recovery after healing.
In 2/10,000 partition/crash trials, barrier-index promotion restored key data but omitted the dedup checkpoint, applying an acknowledged retry twice.
How can promotion guarantee learners durably install deduplication state through the barrier index before serving retried writes?
Given 42-minute catch-up at 83% throughput, atomic key-and-dedup barrier persistence should prevent duplicate retries while retaining ≥80% throughput.
Atomically persist learner keys and dedup state through the barrier; require destination-quorum durability before promotion; test crash/retry safety and throughput.
Repeat 10,000 partition/crash/retry trials with atomic key-and-dedup barrier checkpoints; reject promotion until destination quorum fsyncs the checkpoint.
Across 10,000 crash/partition/retry trials, quorum-fsynced atomic barrier checkpoints yielded zero duplicate retries or lost acknowledged writes.
Provisionally retain learner streaming after its pre-gate 83% result; adopt quorum-fsynced atomic checkpoints against duplicate retries, then rebenchmark throughput.
Offload snapshots to object storage for Raft learners; jointly reconfigure only after quorum-fsynced key-and-dedup barriers.
Can object-storage snapshots reduce source egress while preserving learner catch-up and quorum-fsynced barrier consistency?
Object-storage snapshots halve source egress versus direct streaming while learners catch up within 60 minutes and barrier durability remains intact.
Upload a versioned, checksummed copy-on-write snapshot; compare source egress and catch-up against direct streaming, then fault-inject barrier promotion.
Compare direct and object-store snapshots in 60-minute WriteHot-1 runs; measure source egress, barrier catch-up, and checkpoint integrity.
SnapshotCompare-v1 records WriteHot-1 source-egress bytes, learner barrier-catch-up times, and key/dedup checkpoint checksums for both transfer paths.
Analyze SnapshotCompare-v1 for ≥50% source-egress savings and ≤60-minute catch-up; verify object-store checksums match quorum-fsynced key/dedup barriers.
SnapshotCompare-v1 shows 54% less source egress, 47-minute catch-up, and matching key/dedup barrier checksums with quorum-fsynced learners.
Using SnapshotCompare-v1 baselines, fault-inject stale manifests, truncated objects, and one crash; check egress savings, catch-up, and promotion safety.
In 2/10,000 stale-manifest/crash trials, fsynced barriers promoted stale key state, losing acknowledged writes; retries cut egress savings to 35%.
How can learners bind object-store manifests to Raft snapshot indices and verify complete key/dedup state before barrier promotion?
Raft-index-bound, hash-verified key/dedup manifests should prevent stale promotion; reusing verified blocks may restore ≥50% egress savings from 35%.
Bind immutable snapshot manifests to Raft index, term, and key/dedup hash; reuse verified blocks, then rerun stale-manifest crash tests.
Extend SnapshotCompare-v1 with index/term-bound manifests and block-hash reuse; rerun 10,000 stale-manifest/crash trials and egress measurements.
Index/term-bound manifests yielded zero stale promotions in 10,000 trials; block reuse restored 52% source-egress savings.
Adopt indexed, hash-verified manifests with block reuse; they eliminated observed stale promotions and recovered 52% egress savings.
Combine indexed object snapshots, quorum-fsynced key/dedup barriers, joint-consensus transfer, and foreground-priority streaming throttled at 86% throughput.
Does the integrated migration protocol preserve acknowledgments and ≥80% throughput when crashes, retries, and sustained writes overlap?
Integrated migration yields zero lost acknowledgments or duplicate retries under one crash and ≥80% baseline throughput without failures.
Implement integrated cutover, model-check ownership safety, inject crash/partition/retry faults, and benchmark 60-minute continuous-write throughput.
Run IntegratedCutover-1 with 10,000 crash/partition/retry trials and 60-minute fault-free WriteHot-1 migrations; check acknowledgments, deduplication, and throughput.
IntegratedCutover-1: 10,000 fault trials lost zero acknowledged writes or duplicated retries; 60-minute WriteHot-1 sustained 82% baseline throughput.
Inject partitions and one crash during joint-consensus commit, then replay ambiguous retries; verify single ownership and committed-write survival.
In 2/10,000 partition/crash trials, destination acknowledged retries before joint-config commit; rollback lost those writes and briefly split ownership.
Which durable ownership gate prevents destination acknowledgments before joint-config commit and source reactivation after promotion?
Gating destination acknowledgments on joint-config commit and durably epoch-fencing the source should prevent rollback losses while sustaining ≥80% baseline throughput.
Add a durable ownership gate keyed to committed joint-config index and epoch; rerun fault injection and 60-minute throughput benchmarks.
Repeat 10,000 partition/crash/retry schedules with committed-index ownership gates; measure rollback losses, split ownership, and 60-minute WriteHot-1 throughput.
Committed-index gates yielded zero rollback losses or split ownership in 10,000 trials; WriteHot-1 sustained 81% baseline for 60 minutes.
Adopt committed-index ownership gates; they removed observed rollback losses and split ownership while preserving 81% sustained throughput.
